newsitem.title: INDIA: Cotton-Indian trade sees boom times ahead.
newsitem.headline: Cotton-Indian trade sees boom times ahead.

text.p: India's cash-strapped cotton trade is heading for boom times, driven by a liberal credit policy coinciding with a bumper harvest, traders said on Thursday.
They said the lifting of credit controls on cotton by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) over the weekend was a great relief to traders, who had been facing a severe funds crunch.
"The RBI policy is timely. It will definitely help orderly marketing of cotton," an official of the East India Cotton Association (EICA) said.
The official, who did not want to be named, said the cotton trade had so far been subject to heavy margins by banks and allowed only 30 to 60 percent of their total credit needs.
He said the availability of enough funds would now lead to a quicker turnaround in volumes and help traders to reduce profit margins and pass them on to cotton farmers.
Exporters said the lifting of credit controls would also make more funds available to finance exports.
India has authorised an export of 500,000 bales (170 kg each) from the new crop and traders expect the release of a further quantity later.
In 1995/96, exporters signed up contracts for 1.1 million bales against an authorised quantity of 1.59 million.
Traders said about 400,000 bales could not be contracted for mainly due to late authorisation of exports. The backlog could now be cleared with the availability of more financing, they said.
Traders said new crop arrivals, estimated initially at around 16 million bales, had picked up across India, especially in the northern states of Punjab and Haryana.
India harvested around 16 million bales in 1995/96.
Traders said daily arrivals in the northern region in the week to Thursday rose to 16,000/18,000 bales from 8,000/10,000 bales a week ago, depressing prices.
"Punjab cotton initially climbed up after the RBI policy cheered market sentiment, but the rally lost its steam following the heavy new crop arrivals," said a trader.
In the spot market, Punjab saw-ginned fell 30-35 rupees to 1,625/1,700 rupees per maund (37.32 kg).
Bengal-deshi (ready delivery) settled 30-50 rupees lower at 960/1,020 rupees per maund (37.32 kg). But Gujarat cotton varieties gained on reports of poor arrivals due to unseasonal rains.
In spot, Gujarat Kalyan rose by 100 rupees to 12,900/13,000 rupees per candy (355.56 kg) and Gujarat Sankar-4 (long-staple) by 100 rupees to 20,600/21,300 rupees per candy.
"Prices may ease further in the next few days under the pressure of new crop arrivals," one broker said.
